source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song & Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to critique and fix its own answer made accuracy go down, not up. Multi-agent debate gains were explained by self-consistency: at the same number of responses, plain majority voting beat debate.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7 (after 1 and 2 correction rounds); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. Self-consistency on GSM8K (GPT-3.5): 1 response 76.7, 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2. Debate only slightly above self-consistency at 3 responses and below it at larger equal counts. Oracle-label correction looked large, but the authors call that an oracle result. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changed, correct-to-wrong was more common than wrong-to-correct.
quote: the improvement is evidently not attributed to self-correction, but rather to self-consistency
limits: Table layout in the PDF text was garbled; numbers read from the cleaner rows. Generic 'review your answer' prompts, not scheme-specific CQs. GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 era.
agent_relevance: A CQ test step that is just the model re-judging itself is the weak case. Any critique step has to be compared with plain voting at equal calls, and needs a signal from outside the model.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam & Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing its own answers collapsed performance. A sound external checker gave large gains, and re-sampling with the checker and no critique text kept most of the gain. Self-consistency with 15 samples did not help in these domains.
numbers: Accuracy, 100 instances per domain, columns standard prompt / LLM+LLM binary feedback / LLM+sound verifier binary feedback / sound verifier first-error feedback / sampling with verifier k=25 / self-consistency of 15. Game of 24: 5/3/36/38/42/6. Graph coloring: 16/2/38/37/44/14. Blocksworld: 40/55/60/87/72/42. Mystery Blocksworld: 4/0/10/8/14/4. LLM as verifier: Game of 24 accuracy 87.0%, false positive 10.4% (320/3071), false negative 20.7%; Blocksworld false positive 6.5%, false negative 15.48%; Mystery Blocksworld false positive 18.55%, false negative 97.09% (100/103); Graph coloring false negative 95.8% (113/118). On equations that equal 24 the model marked 79.1% correct but computed 81.6% of them to 24.
limits: Planning and puzzle domains with exact verifiers; GPT-4 only; free-form critiques were full of invented edges and preconditions. Not argumentation tasks.
agent_relevance: Strongest support for letting code, not the model, answer any CQ that has an exact check (recompute a number, check a constraint). Where no sound check exists, extra critique text added little; more independent samples plus a checker did the work.

source: Gou, Shao, Gong et al. (2024) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing, ICLR
finding: Letting the model verify its answer with a search engine or code interpreter and then revise improved results. Removing the tools (model critiques itself only) gave almost nothing.
numbers: Text-Davinci-003, F1 (AmbigNQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA): CoT 58.6 / 74.5 / 46.1; Self-Consistency 58.5 / 74.5 / 47.5; CRITIC 64.9 / 80.6 / 50.5; CRITIC without tool 58.3 / 74.7 / 46.1. Across the two LLMs the model's own critiques changed F1 by -0.03 and +2.33. Maths program synthesis (text-davinci-003) CRITIC +2.1 on one set vs without tool -1.8.
quote: the model's own critiques contribute marginally to the improvement
limits: Text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT era; short factual or maths items. Self-consistency sample count is modest.
agent_relevance: Which CQs code can answer: those that map to search (is the quoted source real, is the expert quoted correctly) or to code (does the number recompute). The tool-grounded checks gave the gain; self-critique alone did not.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen & Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location, Findings of ACL
finding: Models are bad at finding which step of a reasoning trace is wrong, even in clear cases, but fix it well when told where the error is. A small trained classifier found mistakes better than prompting a large model.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks, 300 traces per task (255 wrong, 45 right). Best prompted result: GPT-4 reached only 52.87 overall mistake-finding accuracy with direct step-level prompting. GPT-3.5-Turbo scored between 1.67 and 19.00 on one task depending on prompt style. Backtracking with a given location lifts downstream accuracy, and stays useful at about 60-70% classifier accuracy.
limits: Chain-of-thought traces from PaLM 2; objective tasks (word sorting, object tracking, logic, arithmetic, Dyck). Table text partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Locating the weak point is the hard part and fixing it is the easy part. A CQ points at a place; the test should check that the question's target really is the flawed step.

source: Zhang, Khalifa, Logeswaran et al. (2024) Small Language Models Need Strong Verifiers to Self-Correct Reasoning, Findings of ACL
finding: 7B and 13B models can be trained to refine answers, but only a strong verifier (oracle or GPT-4) tells them when to refine. A weak self-verifier gave small gains or misled the refiner.
numbers: Llama-2-13B-chat and Gemma-7B-it, five math and commonsense datasets. With a GPT-4 verifier the Gemma-7B refiner gained +8.3 accuracy on average. With the model's own fine-tuned verifier the gain was minor, 'if not misguiding the refiner' (paper wording).
limits: Refiner is fine-tuned (not prompt only); math and commonsense only. Exact confusion-matrix cells were garbled in the extracted table and are not used.
agent_relevance: Below about 13B the checker, not the reviser, is the bottleneck. A CQ judge run by a small model will let flawed items through; use code or a larger model as judge.

source: Dhuliawala, Komeili, Xu et al. (2024) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models, Findings of ACL
finding: Verification questions answered independently of the draft beat answering them in the same context (the model copies its own errors). Open questions beat yes/no questions that restate the claim, because the model tends to agree with the stated fact.
numbers: Wiki-Category list task precision (Llama 65B): yes/no verification questions joint 0.15 vs factored 0.19; general (open) questions joint 0.15 vs factored 0.22; rule-based yes/no templates 0.13 vs 0.16. Wikidata list precision: few-shot 0.17, CoVe joint 0.29, two-step 0.36, factored 0.32. Longform FACTSCORE 55.9 -> 71.4 with CoVe.
quote: the model tends to agree with the way the question is stated, even if it was stated incorrectly
limits: Hallucination in lists and biographies, Llama 65B; not argument evaluation. The yes/no gap is modest (3 precision points).
agent_relevance: Format for CQ checks: ask the open form (what did the expert actually say about X?) in a fresh context, not 'is the expert reliable, yes or no' with the claim included. Answer each CQ separately.

source: Singhi, Bansal, Hosseini et al. (2025) When To Solve, When To Verify: Compute-Optimal Problem Solving and Generative Verification for LLM Reasoning, COLM
finding: At a fixed token budget, spending it on more samples with majority vote beat spending it on written verification chains of thought. Verification only wins at large budgets.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B on MATH: the fine-tuned generative verifier needed about 8x the compute to match self-consistency, and 128x the compute to gain 3.8 points over the best self-consistency result (SC plateaus near 128 solutions). Hard problems benefit more, up to 30% relative gain over SC at high budgets. Untuned Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct on MATH and GPQA-Diamond (64 problems) and QwQ-32B on AIME25 show the same shape: SC better at low budget, verifier better at high budget. Fine-tuned verifier needed up to 16x less compute than the untuned one.
limits: Maths and GPQA with answers that can be voted on. The verifier is a generated chain of thought, not scheme-specific CQs.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 2 for the generic case: a model-run test step must beat voting at equal tokens, and at small budgets it usually does not. Use CQ tests when answers cannot be voted on, on hard items, or when code does the check.

source: Luo, Lin, Liu, Shu, Zhu, Shang & Meng (2023) Critique Ability of Large Language Models (CriticBench)
finding: Critiquing is hard and near chance for small and medium models; it separates from random guessing only in large models. Self-critique is harder still, and critique is worst where the model is least certain.
numbers: CriticBench: 3K queries with correct and incorrect responses from math (GSM8K), code (HumanEval) and QA (TruthfulQA); PaLM-2, LLaMA, LLaMA-2 and ChatGPT in several sizes. Figure caption: all medium-sized or smaller models perform akin to random guessing on all tasks. Exact accuracies sit in figures and were not extracted.
limits: 2023 models; PaLM-2 T-shirt sizes are not parameter counts. Figures only, so no numeric threshold.
agent_relevance: Supports a size floor for model-run critique steps (gap 7). It does not name 70B.

source: Li, Li, Chang & Wu (2025) Don't Take the Premise for Granted: Evaluating the Premise Critique Ability of LLMs (PCBench)
finding: Models rarely flag a flawed premise unless told to look for errors. The explicit instruction raises detection a lot, so a plain 'check this' prompt is not the same as no prompt. Detection falls with difficulty.
numbers: 15 LLMs. Proactive rate (no hint): GPT-4o 11.0, DeepSeek-V3 40.5, o4-mini 4.0. Assisted rate (told to check): GPT-4.1 73.2, Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking 77.9, o4-mini 74.2. Qwen3 non-thinking 8B to 235B: assisted 59.9 -> 70.0, proactive 20.6 -> 24.7. Qwen3-235B thinking: proactive 35.3, assisted 70.1, proactive answer length 3629 tokens. On Hard problems even the best models stay near or below 30% proactive. Reasoning models often noticed the flaw in their thinking but did not state it in the final answer.
limits: Maths word problems with injected errors (4 error types), judged by o3-mini-high (checked on 240 items against humans). Critique of premises, not of argument schemes.
agent_relevance: A mandatory CQ step in the scaffold fixes the 'never looks' failure but does not guarantee finding it (assisted rates cap near 70-78%). Reasoning-model flaws seen in thinking need an explicit 'state it' rule.

source: Turkstra, Nabhani & Al-Khatib (2025) TriLLaMA at CQs-Gen 2025: A Two-Stage LLM-Based System for Critical Question Generation, ArgMining workshop
finding: An LLM used to judge whether a critical question is useful was strongly biased to say yes. Making the judge debate or deliberate did not help. Scaling the question writer from 8B to 405B gave little.
numbers: LLaMA 3.1 8B / 70B / 405B, 34 test interventions, 340 generated questions. The best classifier (70B zero-shot) labelled 8.4 of 10 questions Useful on average; of 180 questions that received gold labels only 44.4% were Useful (22.8% Unhelpful, 15% Invalid, 17.8% unscorable). Ceiling for a perfect selector: 73.5. Test scores: zero-shot judge 53.9 (55.9 after manual relabel), debate 52.0, deliberation 37.3. Generation validation: few-shot 8B 67.2 vs 405B 68.5 (+1.3 points for 50 times the size). Classifier binary accuracy, zero-shot 8B/70B/405B: 58.2/65.8/62.4; few-shot 60.9/64.4/59.2.
limits: The judge rates usefulness of questions against similarity-matched references, not the truth of an argument. Small test set (34). Authors note debate mostly adds tokens.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence of a yes-bias in an LLM acting as CQ judge (gaps 5 and 9). Debate formats cost more tokens and did not fix it.

source: El Baff (2025) CriticalBrew at CQs-Gen 2025: Collaborative Multi-Agent Generation and Evaluation of Critical Questions for Arguments, ArgMining workshop
finding: Multi-agent question generation (agents debate then reflect) beat a single zero-shot LLM for 8B, 24B and 70B models, while the choice of LLM judge format made no difference. A 24B model matched a 70B model, so there was no 70B cliff here.
numbers: Validation overall score: Llama 8B best 0.71 (about 3 points above its single-LLM baseline), Mistral 24B 0.78 and Llama 70B 0.78 (4-5 points above baseline). Share of items with all three questions useful: 0.42 for 8B vs 0.53-0.58 for 24B and 70B. Agent count significant for all three models (p<0.05); thinking pattern significant for 8B and 70B. Test set (N=34): only the best Mistral 24B run (3 agents) beat the shared-task baseline, at 0.55.
limits: Question writing, not argument verification. More agents means more tokens and there is no token-matched comparison. Test gains were smaller than validation gains.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no 70B threshold for generating CQs; medium models do as well as large ones. The gains tracked the number of agents (tokens), a warning for gap 2.

source: Nguyen & Nguyen (2025) Tdnguyen at CQs-Gen 2025: Adapt Large Language Models with Multi-Step Reasoning for Critical Questions Generation, ArgMining workshop
finding: Zero-shot and one-shot chain of thought beat a plain GPT-4o-mini baseline; tree of thoughts was no better and cost over 20 times more. DeepSeek-R1, Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B were also run but results are only in bar charts.
numbers: 30 runs on the validation set with GPT-4o-mini. Token cost: zero-shot CoT 2.17M in / 1.10M out, $0.98; one-shot CoT 5.20M / 0.90M, $1.27; tree of thoughts 97.39M / 10.94M, $21.10. The LLaMA-3-8B baseline lagged all GPT-4o-mini methods. One-shot CoT best on validation, but zero-shot CoT and ToT slightly beat it on the hidden test.
limits: Automatic similarity scoring (threshold 0.6); per-method scores sit in a figure not extracted. No scheme information used.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: even with R1 and Qwen3 added there are no usable numbers. Cost note: simple CoT gave the gain at about 5% of the ToT cost.

source: COGNAC team (2025) COGNAC at CQs-Gen 2025: Generating Critical Questions with LLM-Assisted Prompting and Multiple RAG Variants, ArgMining workshop
finding: Adding scheme descriptions to the prompt gave no consistent gain in question quality. The biggest gain came from examples retrieved by similarity, not from schemes.
numbers: Validation score (unscorable counted as failures): baseline prompt 0.62; improved zero-shot 0.76; 2-shot random examples 0.78; retrieved examples by intervention 0.83, plus scheme descriptions 0.81; retrieved annotated examples 0.79, plus scheme descriptions 0.82. Test: examples-only run 0.63 with manual review (second place); scheme variants 0.60-0.62. Authors say hand-written scheme descriptions lacked nuance and no standard definitions exist.
limits: Graded by similarity to reference questions; validation differences of 0.01-0.03 are within noise; test set is 34 interventions.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (partial): scheme text in the prompt is not clearly better than no scheme text for question quality, matching K04.

source: ARG2ST team (2025) ARG2ST at CQs-Gen 2025: Critical Questions Generation through LLMs and Usefulness-based Selection, ArgMining workshop
finding: In a prompt ablation with Mixtral-8x7B and Llama-3-8B the plain base prompt was best. Adding the argument's scheme labels gave the worst results across models, and adding CQ definitions did not catch up with the base prompt.
numbers: Base prompt best overall. Among definitions, describing non-useful questions was more reliable than describing useful ones or both, but still below base. The schemes prompt was worst for both models. Qwen-2.5-7B was dropped because it scored below the other two on all prompts. Authors suspect scheme labels hurt because they do not say which part of the text each scheme covers.
limits: Exact scores are in an appendix table not extracted. Scheme labels came from gold annotations, not a router. Same shared task and 34-item test.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: giving the model the correct scheme label did not help question quality, so routing accuracy may matter less for generation than expected.

source: Kanadan, Kiesel, Heinrich & Stein (2025) Webis at CQs-Gen 2025: Prompting and Reranking for Critical Questions, ArgMining workshop
finding: Generating six candidates with two small models and keeping the top three by a fine-tuned ModernBERT usefulness classifier beat generation alone. Scheme-aware prompting was dropped because it did not help.
numbers: Gemma 2 prompting only: sample 0.53, validation 0.72, test 0.49. Gemma 2 + Phi-4 with reranker trained on validation plus 67.8k self-labelled questions: 0.67 / 0.84 / 0.57 (rank 5; 58 Useful after manual review of 12 unscorable). Reranker trained on validation only: 0.56 / 0.82 / 0.48. Scheme-integration row (Gemma 2): sample 0.60, validation 0.72, equal to plain prompting on validation although the text says it scored lower in tests. Short interventions gave generic questions.
limits: Test result partly based on manual relabelling; labels come from similarity to references; models 3B to 14B.
agent_relevance: A small trained selector over several candidates is a cheap code-side filter (gap 3). The scheme-prompt table and text disagree, so count it as no gain.

source: ELLIS Alicante team (2025) CQ templates per scheme, appendix table of ELLIS Alicante at CQs-Gen 2025
finding: The winning team's appendix prints condensed critical-question templates for the schemes. These are shortened paraphrases in the style of Walton, not the book text.
numbers: Analogy: Are the two cases similar in relevant respects? Are there significant differences that undermine the analogy? Is the conclusion in the known case well established? Cause to effect: Is there sufficient evidence that the cause reliably produces the effect? Could other factors intervene? Is the link correlation rather than proven causation? Expert opinion: How credible is the expert? Is the expert an authority in the relevant field? What exactly did the expert assert? Is the expert personally reliable? Three to six questions per scheme.
limits: Table columns were scrambled in PDF extraction; rows matched by content. Not the Walton 2008 text; the book remains unopened.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 10 (partial): short lists for expert opinion, analogy and cause can be coded as slot templates. They need rewording to the argument, as the 39.44% hand-edit rate (c06) shows.

source: ARG2ST team (2025) Table 7: scheme counts in the CQs-Gen validation set
finding: In the real political-debate data of the shared task, example and practical reasoning dominate. Analogy, expert opinion and authority are rare.
numbers: 28 normalized scheme names in the validation set: example 175, practical reasoning 135, cause to effect 55, consequences 38, sign 25, verbal classification 25, circumstantial ad hominem 22, fear appeal 14, analogy 11, expert opinion 10, position to know 10, values 10, popular opinion 8, alternatives 6, popular practice 6, authority 4, bias 4, direct ad hominem 2.
limits: Counts are scheme annotations on debate speech (US2016, Moral Maze), not on puzzles or reasoning tasks. They say nothing yet about ARC, BrainTeaser or novelty items.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: for debate-like input, example, practical reasoning, cause and consequences matter most. For ARC and BrainTeaser we need our own count of which scheme types the agent's reasoning steps use; this paper cannot supply it.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Argumentation scheme page, listing the Walton, Reed & Macagno (2008) expert-opinion questions (secondary, fetched through a summariser)
finding: The page lists six critical questions for argument from expert opinion and none for analogy or cause. The analogy and post hoc pages checked do not cite Walton's CQs either.
numbers: Expert opinion: Expertise (How credible is E as an expert source?), Field (Is E an expert in the field that A is in?), Opinion (What did E assert that implies A?), Trustworthiness (Is E personally reliable as a source?), Consistency (Is A consistent with what other experts assert?), Backup evidence (Is E's assertion based on evidence?). The page names 37 schemes as a selection from the book's larger set.
limits: Encyclopedia page read through a summariser tool, which may have trimmed text; secondary source. The analogy and cause lists from the book itself remain unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the six expert-opinion questions can be coded now. The analogy and cause lists still need the book or a Walton paper.

source: Ballon, Vanhoyweghen, Kim et al. (2026) Big-Big-SycoBench: A Benchmark to Detect Sycophancy Through Model Responses to Valid vs. Invalid Arguments
finding: Frontier models differ hugely in whether they update on a valid argument and whether they cave to an invalid one. The two rates are separate, so a high acceptance rate alone is not a fault and a low one is not a virtue.
numbers: 450 text artefacts, 5,400 arguments (valid or invalid), 12 annotators. Each model scored each artefact 20 times for a baseline, and a revision counted only if it beat that noise. Compliance with invalid / responsiveness to valid, percent: GPT-6 Astra 0/88, Opus 5.5 1/32, GLM-5.3 9/77, Kimi K3 13/76, Grok 4.7 20/89, GPT-5.5 22/92, GPT-5.6 Terra 28/90; GPT-4o compliance 95. Overall: responsiveness 88-95% for seven of ten models.
limits: Scores the quality rating of artefacts, not CQ answering. The 2026 model names will drift. Arguments were written to move a score.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: acceptance bias is model-specific and measurable. Measure compliance (flawed passes) and responsiveness (valid objection accepted) on our own seeded set, per model, before trusting any LLM CQ judge.

source: Fox, Markham, Lail & Karotsieris (2026) LLM Judges Verify Presence, Not Absence: Omission Blindness in AI Clinical Notes and What Recovers It
finding: LLM judges can spot added or altered content but are near chance at spotting what is missing. Turning the check into a closed 'list the facts, then verify each is present' procedure recovered detection.
numbers: 500 single-error note pairs (298 omission, 202 added or altered). Paired discrimination 0.79-0.94 for added or altered content vs 0.50-0.63 for omissions across eight judge designs. Wording changes, voting and GEPA prompt optimisation did not fix it. Per-fact pipeline flagged 24.6% of omission notes at 2.7% false alarms; one evolved-prompt call flagged 36.9% at 6.2% false alarms (p=0.002) at about a tenth of the cost.
limits: Clinical notes, not arguments. Omissions whose fact is restated elsewhere in the note defeat both methods.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: many CQs ask what is missing (is there backup evidence, was a confound considered). A closed checklist ('quote the sentence that supplies X, or write NONE') should beat an open 'is anything missing?' check.

source: Naik, Shabadi, Alur & Naik (2026) Do We Need Frontier Models to Verify Mathematical Proofs?
finding: Smaller open models are not much worse than frontier models at judging proofs but are much less consistent, and prompt choice matters a lot. An ensemble of specialised prompts closed most of the gap.
numbers: Four open-source and two frontier LLMs on human-graded competition proofs. Smaller models were up to 10% behind in accuracy and up to 25% more inconsistent across repeated judgments. An LLM-guided prompt search gave an ensemble worth up to +9.1% accuracy and +15.9% self-consistency; Qwen3.5-35B reached the level of Gemini 3.1 Pro.
limits: Math proofs with human grades; the prompt search needs labelled data.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no clean size cliff; the problem is reliability of the judge. Repeat each CQ check and take agreement.

source: HiTZ (2026) Critical Questions Leaderboard (Hugging Face space) and Benchmarking_CQs-Gen repository
finding: The public leaderboard stores scores in a private results dataset. The code and README were readable but no scores for 2026 frontier or reasoning models could be retrieved. The only reasoning-model runs found are DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-8B charts in the Tdnguyen shared-task paper.
numbers: Task rule: each question scores 1/3 if it matches a Useful reference at similarity 0.65 or higher; unmatched questions are 'not able to evaluate'. The results dataset (HiTZ/results_public) answered 'Invalid username or password'.
limits: Negative result: absence of data is not evidence about 2026 models. The web search quota ran out, so the search for 2026 follow-up papers used only the Hugging Face paper index and the ArgMining 2025 volume.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. To close it we would have to run recent models on the public validation set ourselves.
